newsitem.title: UK: New division on Europe plagues Major's poll battle.
newsitem.headline: New division on Europe plagues Major's poll battle.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives were rocked by fresh divisions over their European policy on Tuesday, frustrating their efforts to mount a fightback against Labour leader Tony Blair ahead of the May 1 election.

Ministers unleashed furious attacks on Blair, accusing him of hypocrisy over education policy and naivety over economic plans, and prepared to welcome what are expected to be favourable figures on unemployment to be published on Wednesday.

But at a campaign news conference, they were forced to divert their attention from these issues by news that a Conservative vice-chairwoman, Angela Rumbold, was defying Prime Minister John Major's policy on the single European currency.
Rumbold, head of the party's candidates' department, said in an election address to her south London constituents that she would under no circumstances vote to give up the pound sterling.

"No to more powers for Brussels. No to a single currency. Yes to a referendum before any further steps of constitutional importance are taken," she wrote in direct contradiction of Major's official "wait and see" policy.
Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine tried to make light of Rumbold's defiance.

"There are views across the whole spectrum of politics in every party about this issue, and so there should be," he said. "We are not going to conduct a witch-hunt of the views of individual candidates."
But Blair, whose party leads the Conservatives by 18 points in the latest poll, said Major's party would be "like ferrets in a sack" over Europe if they won on May 1.
"You can't have strong leadership with a divided Conservative Party. They can't fight for Britain's interests if they are fighting among themselves," he said.
Paddy Ashdown, leader of the minority Liberal Democrats, said: "The Conservative ship is breaking up. John Major is alone on the bridge and the crew are running for the lifeboats."
Heseltine, whose vivid choice of phrase and combative manner make him one of the Conservatives' most effective campaigners, launched a two-pronged attack on Blair.

He said the Labour leader's decision to send one of his sons to a school that has opted out of local authority control -- even though Labour was originally opposed to allowing schools to do that -- was pure hypocrisy.
"I can't stand the hypocrisy of a man who says he would deny choice in education and then applies that choice for his own children," Heseltine said.
"A man who does that is not fit to discuss this nation's education policies, let alone be Prime Minister," he added.
Heseltine also described Blair's plan to cut youth unemployment by 250,000 using fund from a "windfall" tax on excess profits of privatised companies as "phoney".

He said Labour plans to introduce a minimum wage would lose far more jobs than such a scheme could ever create. "A manifesto based on such a shaky foundation is no basis for trust. It's quite simply a fraud," he said.
Blair, who on Sunday promised a more positive campaign, saying abuse by politicians against each other turned voters off, described Conservative attacks on him as "negative" and "nasty".
Social Security Secretary Peter Lilley also attacked Labour employment plans, provoking speculation that Wednesday's official jobless figures will show another sizeable drop.
